tldr: A bimanual robot with multi-fingered hands safely learns five distinct 3-ball juggling patterns online in just minutes of physical interaction, starting from an imperfect mathematical model.
hero_caption: The overall hierarchical system architecture. When skill commands arrive from the orchestrator, the memory-based learner blends real-world experience with an imperfect prior model to correct throw commands, while safe joint trajectories are generated under mutually reachable set (MRS) constraints.
overview:
The discrepancy between simulations or analytical models and the physical world (the sim2real gap) is especially severe in dynamic manipulation involving rapid, sequential contacts. In multi-fingered robot juggling, subtle variations in grasp pose during each catch or slight changes in fingertip friction and release timing can drastically disrupt throw outcomes, making purely precomputed models insufficient for sustained success. On the other hand, exploring from scratch on physical hardware (such as via reinforcement learning) takes far too long and risks damaging the robot.

To address this, the authors realized that even an imperfect model's gradient (its trend of variation) serves as a powerful prior for learning. They developed "regularized memory-based learning," which stores past throw outcomes in memory and builds a local linear regression model while regularizing toward the first-order derivative of the prior model where data is sparse. Furthermore, to ensure the robot can safely reach subsequent catching actions without violating joint limits even after an executed motion, they computed an offline "mutually reachable set (MRS)" and integrated it into the planner's constraints.

In experiments on the bimanual robot "AthenaZero," starting from a coarse prior model that could not sustain even a single cycle on its own, the robot learned the cascade pattern in just 53 seconds of active physical interaction (around 5 minutes in total, excluding human ball-retrieval time). The framework also successfully learned and continuously executed five challenging patterns—including tennis, half-shower, shower, and box—along with transitions between them within minutes.
contributions: Proposed regularized local memory-based learning that uses the first-order gradient of an imperfect prior model as a regularizer, enabling immediate on-robot adaptation without uninformed physical exploration.

Introduced the mutually reachable set (MRS) to prevent joint position, velocity, and acceleration limits from being violated across consecutive high-speed actions, ensuring dynamic safety during physical learning.
Demonstrated that a bimanual robot with multi-fingered hands can master five canonical 3-ball juggling patterns (including cascade and shower) in under several minutes of real-world interaction each.
Showed that acquired throwing skills can be reused across different juggling patterns, significantly accelerating the learning of new skills.

sections.heading: Tackling dynamic manipulation: Learning without a perfect model
sections.summary: Juggling involves high-speed, intermittent contacts, making it exceptionally hard to model since minor errors compound rapidly. This work introduces an online learning framework that leverages an imperfect model unable to complete even a single cycle as prior knowledge, safely and quickly adapting directly on physical hardware.
sections.details:
Prior knowledge from simulations or analytical models offers a great starting point for real-world adaptation, but slight deviations from reality prove fatal in high-speed, contact-rich tasks. In multi-fingered robot juggling, small shifts in catch location or finger release timing significantly alter ball trajectories. Because real-world conditions shift continuously due to daily wear or humidity, developing a perfect analytical model from the start is fundamentally limited.

Conversely, exploring on hardware from scratch (as in conventional reinforcement learning) takes too long and poses a high risk of hardware damage. The paper focuses on a core insight: even when far from reality, a model is extremely useful as prior knowledge for understanding trends of change. The framework adopts regularized memory-based learning, which fits a local model from physical interaction data in well-explored regions and safely extrapolates using the prior model's gradient where experience is sparse.

Continuous real-world learning also demands safety. An individual throw might stay within joint limits, but the arm's terminal position and velocity could prevent it from moving to the next catch without exceeding joint or deceleration bounds. To eliminate this issue, the authors precomputed a "mutually reachable set (MRS)"—a set of states that can safely transition to all subsequent actions—and enforced it as an online planner constraint.

captions.F1: The overall system architecture. The orchestrator on the left manages the global schedule, while inside the skill executor at the center, the memory-based learner and the MRS-constrained planner collaborate to achieve safe and accurate throws.

sections.heading: From dedicated paddles to multi-fingered hands: Reusing learned experience
sections.summary: Traditional robot juggling largely relied on model-based control with passively stable cups or paddles, but multi-fingered hands introduce massive contact uncertainty. Building on the heritage of memory-based learning, this work enables online real-world adaptation framed around reusable skills.
sections.details:
Robot juggling has a rich history. Early milestones, such as Shannon's juggling machine and subsequent systems using specialized end-effectors like cups or paddles, leveraged passive contact mechanics to achieve robust operation without high-precision learning.

However, moving to anthropomorphic, multi-fingered hands complicates the mechanics enormously. Complex phenomena—including friction, elasticity, impact, and release timing—render analytical modeling extremely difficult. While prior studies investigated iterative learning control or locally weighted learning for trajectory correction, they often focused on updating entire open-loop throwing sequences offline between episodes.

Recent work by Ploeger et al. similarly used first-order information from analytical models for regularization, but updated entire open-loop throw sequences across trials. In contrast, this approach formulates throwing as a reusable skill conditioned on the ball state observed from preceding actions. This formulation allows identical skills to be shared across distinct juggling patterns, reusing prior experience and facilitating real-time online learning during active juggling.

sections.heading: Mastered in minutes: Rapidly acquiring five patterns on physical hardware
sections.summary: The bimanual robot learned the cascade pattern within 53 seconds of physical interaction (around 7 resets, excluding ball retrieval), mastered multi-pattern transitions, and tackled high-precision patterns like the shower and box. Ablation studies confirmed that MRS constraints are vital to preventing hardware damage.
sections.details:
Physical experiments were conducted on "AthenaZero," a low-inertia bimanual robot developed by the RAI Institute. Equipped with two 3-fingered hands (opening and closing in ~80 ms) and a head-mounted RGB-D camera, it juggles three 130 g beanbag balls.

- Rapid cascade learning (Section 2.2): Excluding manual ball-retrieval time, the robot mastered the cascade pattern (sustaining 5 consecutive cycles) within an average of 53 seconds of physical operation (about 7 resets). The entire process took roughly 5 minutes. Throwing errors visibly converged with each trial.
- Skill reuse and pattern transitions (Section 2.3): In tasks requiring transitions across tennis, half-shower, and cascade patterns, throwing skills learned in tennis transferred directly. As a result, subsequent patterns were acquired and sustained after only 2 to 3 resets (averaging 75 seconds of active interaction).
- Conquering high-precision patterns (Section 2.4): Low-throw patterns with short flight times, such as the shower and the horizontal toss in the box, undercut visual feedback latency (~0.1 s), forcing open-loop catches. Despite demanding extreme throwing accuracy, learning drastically narrowed landing dispersion, enabling multi-cycle completions.
- Safety validation (Section 2.5): An ablation analysis removing MRS constraints across 7,578 logged planner queries revealed that without MRS, 89.0% of calculated solutions fell into dangerous states—either unreachable from the prior state or non-survivable due to inevitable limit violations in subsequent motions. This demonstrates that MRS is crucial for hardware preservation.

captions.F2: Learning curves across juggling patterns. The horizontal axis indicates the number of resets, and the vertical axis shows consecutive successful throws. Cascade (A) and multi-skill transitions (B) reach the target threshold (dashed line) within 7–8 resets, while shower (C) and box (D) also show substantial gains in throw counts.
captions.F3: Evolution of ball trajectories and landing point distributions across learning. Moving from left (initial resets) to right (after learning), the throw landing points (scatter points) concentrate tightly around the target location.
captions.F5: The mutually reachable set (translucent blue polytope) in joint phase space alongside target transition states from the planner. Without MRS constraints, many unreachable (brown) or non-survivable (purple) commands that violate joint limits are generated.

sections.heading: Lessons from real-world adaptation: Toward hardware-software co-evolution
sections.summary: This work demonstrates that pairing imperfect models with physical experience is remarkably effective for dynamic tasks. It also highlights key practical challenges, such as sensory latency limitations in open-loop regimes and shifting contact conditions on physical hardware over time.
sections.details:
A core takeaway from these experiments is that no matter how poorly an initial model performs, having access to its gradient information can dramatically accelerate learning. Furthermore, specialized mechanisms (like paddles) and general-purpose multi-fingered hands are not mutually exclusive; the authors emphasize a hybrid perspective where good mechanical design keeps behavior somewhat predictable, and physical adaptation bridges the remaining gap.

A practical operational challenge encountered was shifting friction: dust accumulation on palms and fingertips, changes in ambient humidity, or even simple hand cleaning altered friction enough to break skills that worked the previous day. This reinforces the necessity of continuous online learning frameworks over static zero-shot policies.

Remaining limitations include failures induced by vision latency in patterns like the shower and box. When flight times are excessively short, vision-only catches reach their limit. Integrating tactile sensing or proprioception for instantaneous reactive control will be critical. Future extensions also include handling rotating objects such as clubs and expanding MRS to heavy-duty tasks with large contact forces.

sections.heading: Under the hood: Integrating regularized memory learning, MRS, and fast vision
sections.summary: The proposed system integrates three core components: trajectory planning with a mutually reachable set (MRS) satisfying physical constraints, a local linear regression learner regularized by the prior model's gradient, and high-speed visual perception combining prompt-based segmentation with FastGICP.
sections.details:
- Safe motion synthesis and MRS (Section 4.1): Motions execute as sequences of throwing and catching skills. Transition states (position, velocity, acceleration) connecting consecutive skills maintain acceleration continuity to respect actuator bandwidth. The mutually reachable set (MRS) is computed offline using B-splines to evaluate forward and backward reachable sets, taking their intersection as a convex polytope $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{s} \leq \mathbf{m}$. Because the online planner only searches for target states inside this polytope, the robot is structurally guaranteed never to reach a dead end for the next action.

- Regularized memory-based learning (Section 4.2): For a throwing skill, the learner calculates a corrected target landing position $\mathbf{u}$ based on the prior catch state $\mathbf{x}$ and the desired landing position $\mathbf{y}_d$. It queries the $k$-nearest neighbors from memory to identify a local linear model $(\mathbf{C}, \mathbf{D}, \mathbf{d})$ weighted by an RBF kernel. A regularization term (weight $\gamma$) penalizing deviations from the prior model $\mathbf{f}_0$'s gradient is added to the objective. This allows safe extrapolation along the prior gradient when data is sparse. Command updates are solved as a Levenberg-Marquardt-style regularized quadratic program, preventing overly abrupt command shifts.

- High-speed vision engine (Section 4.3): Balls are segmented from RGB-D images using EfficientTAM, prompted by point clicks on just a few calibration frames. Extracted point clouds are aligned with CAD models via FastGICP at high speed, and ballistic parabolic trajectories under gravity are fitted to predict future landing positions and times. New objects can be tracked immediately with a few prompt points without model retraining.

captions.F6: Conceptual diagram of safe skill synthesis via the mutually reachable set (MRS). When the task planner maps command $u$ to joint target states, restricting solutions within the MRS polytope guarantees that the downstream trajectory generator can transition to and from states without violating joint position, velocity, or acceleration limits.

sections.heading: Appendix: Target configurations and per-joint MRS polytopes
sections.summary: The appendix provides detailed configurations for the spatial targets shared across juggling skills, the explicit polytope geometries of the MRS across all AthenaZero joints, and the planner's optimization formulation.
sections.details:
The appendix shares extensive implementation details. Twelve spatial targets (six per arm: $R1 \sim R6, L1 \sim L6$) were designed to simultaneously accommodate arm kinematic limits, camera field of view (FoV), and physical clearance to prevent mid-air ball collisions.

Additionally, the construction results of the MRS for all seven joints of AthenaZero's right arm (RJ1–RJ7) are documented, demonstrating how the intersection of forward and backward reachable sets defines a robust "survivable region" in joint phase space (position, velocity, acceleration). In the task planner's optimization, dynamics-informed constraints are applied, such as enforcing an equality constraint setting end-effector acceleration to gravitational acceleration $g$ at release to ensure smooth ball detachment from the fingertips.

captions.F7: Layout of the 12 spatial target positions (R1–R6, L1–L6) shared across juggling skills. Targets active for each pattern are highlighted in red, positioned to remain inside the camera FOV while preventing mid-air ball collisions.

takeaways: An inaccurate model is not a useless model: Even if an imperfect model cannot succeed zero-shot, its first-order gradient provides an exceptionally rapid foundation for physical adaptation.

Blending local regression with prior gradients: Fitting real-world experience where data is abundant and regularizing toward prior gradients where data is sparse eliminates blind, high-risk exploration.

MRS is vital for high-speed physical adaptation: Dynamic safety requires more than executing a single motion; verifying safe transitions into subsequent actions via the mutually reachable set unlocks hardware limits without risk of damage.

Modular skills enable direct transfer: Decomposing tasks into state-conditioned skills rather than an end-to-end policy makes transferring acquired experience across multiple distinct patterns straightforward.
limitations: Sensor and control latency bottlenecks: In ultra-fast, low-throw trajectories (e.g., horizontal throws in the shower) where flight times drop below 100 ms, visual tracking cannot keep up, forcing open-loop catches that cap success rates.
Contact discontinuities: Secondary contacts between the ball and fingertips during release introduce localized non-linearities and discontinuities, occasionally stalling local linear regression.

Vulnerability to physical surface shifts: Environmental changes like palm dust buildup or humidity fluctuations require relearning, as real-time tactile feedback has not yet been integrated to absorb these variations.
